docs.title: DM² Lab Wiki
docs.text:
Welcome to the DM² Lab internal wiki!

This wiki collects practical information for lab members, including onboarding guidelines, lab management procedures, experimental protocols, and shared technical resources.

The goal of this wiki is to ensure consistency, reproducibility, and efficient collaboration across projects in the lab.

docs.title: Running EEG Experiments
docs.text:
This page describes standard procedures for running EEG experiments in the DM² Lab.

All experimenters are expected to follow these guidelines to ensure data quality, participant safety, and consistency across studies.

The procedures below apply to typical EEG experiments involving decision-making tasks and behavioural responses.

docs.title: Overview of a Standard EEG Session
docs.text:
A standard EEG session consists of the following stages:

  1. Preparation before the participant arrives
  2. Participant briefing and consent
  3. EEG cap fitting and electrode preparation
  4. Training block
  5. Main experiment (multiple blocks)
  6. Breaks and monitoring during the session
  7. Session completion and data saving

At the end of each session, make sure to clean all EEG equipment, turn off the system, and place the battery on charge before leaving the lab.

docs.title: Check EEG Recording Mac
docs.text:
• Start the Mac computer (Password: credentials are provided internally.)
  • Set up the battery (see EEG setup instructions)
  • Open Active on the Mac
  • Navigate to the PSY 600 folder and load config32

docs.title: Check Stimulation Computer
docs.text:
• Windows version PIN/Password: credentials are provided internally.

  • Ubuntu version Password: credentials are provided internally.

Please use the Ubuntu version if your experiment is run via Psychtoolbox and requires precise timing.

  • Launch MATLAB (if your experiment uses Psychtoolbox)
  • Navigate to the correct experiment folder
  • Run the main task script to confirm that the task launches correctly
  • Verify that triggers are sent correctly (if applicable)

docs.title: Electrode Preparation
docs.text:
• Fill syringes with conductive gel
  • Prepare small pieces of tape for securing external electrodes
  • Attach round adhesive stickers to external electrodes
  • Prepare alcohol swabs

docs.title: Check Paperwork
docs.text:
• Prepare the participant information sheet
  • Prepare the consent form
  • Confirm the participant ID

docs.title: EEG Preparation and Cap Fitting
docs.text:
• Ask the participant to take a seat
  • Explain that an EEG cap will be fitted to measure brain activity
  • Explain that additional electrodes will be placed externally near the eyes and on the earlobes

docs.title: Purpose of External Electrodes
docs.text:
• Eye activity generates strong electrical signals
  • These signals are recorded to help remove eye-related artefacts during analysis

docs.title: Key Points to Emphasize
docs.text:
• The procedure is non-invasive
  • The participant may stop or ask questions at any time
  • Participant comfort is a priority

docs.title: Training Block
docs.text:
Training can usually be conducted while electrode preparation is ongoing.

  • After attaching the external electrodes, allow the participant to start the training block
  • Launch the training task on the stimulation computer
  • Enter participant details as required
  • Read out task instructions in a conversational manner and ensure the participant understands the task

docs.title: Main Experiment
docs.text:
Upon completion of the training block, instructions for the main experiment will appear.

  • Read out instructions in a conversational manner
  • Encourage questions and clarify any misunderstandings
  • Briefly summarise the key task requirements

docs.title: Starting Each Block
docs.text:
When ready to start a block:

  • Confirm that the participant is comfortable and ready
  • Leave the EEG recording chamber and close the door
  • Start the EEG recording and enter the subject number using a consistent naming convention (e.g. Sub001_Block1)
  • Click Pause to begin EEG recording
  • Start the first block of trials on the stimulation computer

Save EEG recordings separately for each block.

docs.title: During Each Block
docs.text:
• Monitor incoming EEG data and participant performance
  • Observe response accuracy and behavioural patterns

If responses suggest a misunderstanding:

  • Allow the participant to complete the current block
  • Clarify instructions before the next block begins

docs.title: Between Blocks
docs.text:
• Stop the EEG recording
  • Save the data file using the correct naming convention
  • Check in with the participant:
  • How are you doing?
  • Do you need a short break or some water?
  • Do you have any questions?

  • Are you managing to blink during the slider periods?

  • Start the next block when the participant is ready

Repeat this procedure for each block.

docs.title: Session Completion
docs.text:
After the final block:

  • Stop and save the EEG recording
  • Confirm that all data files are saved correctly
  • Remove the EEG cap and electrodes
  • Clean all equipment according to lab procedures
  • Thank the participant for their time

docs.title: General Notes
docs.text:
• Maintain a calm and professional tone throughout the session
  • Document any deviations from standard procedures
  • Record technical issues or unusual events
  • Ensure that all data are securely backed up after the session

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
Welcome to the DM² Lab.

This page provides an overview of essential information for new lab members to help you get started smoothly.

docs.title: Before You Begin
docs.text:
Please complete the following steps as early as possible:

  • Finish the required Health and Safety induction
  • Obtain card access to the G. E. Fogg building and any laboratories you will use
  • Apply for out-of-hours access if you plan to work outside typical working hours (08:00–18:00)

docs.title: Lab Checklist
docs.text:
Make sure that you have:

  • Been added to the lab Microsoft Teams chat
  • Access to the lab’s shared folders and GitHub repositories
  • Started reading key papers to familiarise yourself with the lab’s research focus and methods

docs.title: Practical First Steps
docs.text:
• Set up the required softwares (see Softwares)
  • Read project-specific documentation and protocols (if applicable)
  • Attend the weekly lab meeting and joint lab meetings (see Lab Management)
  • Attend departmental seminars whenever possible

docs.title: Recommended Reading
docs.text:
Specific reading lists may be provided by your supervisor or project lead. New lab members are encouraged to discuss recommended papers with other members of the lab.

If anything is unclear, please contact Lucie or other members of the lab — questions are always welcome.

docs.title: Lab Management
docs.text: This page outlines general lab organisation and management practices in the DM² Lab.

docs.title: Meetings
docs.text: The DM² Lab maintains a regular meeting structure to support discussion, collaboration, and project development.

docs.title: Weekly Meetings (Wednesdays, 4:00 pm)
docs.text:
Two meeting formats alternate on a bi-weekly basis:

  • Lab Meeting (bi-weekly) Lab members take turns presenting and discussing recent research papers relevant to the lab’s research interests.

  • Joint Lab Meeting (bi-weekly) Project presentations and discussions involving members from across the department. If you would like to present, please contact Keiji to book a slot.

docs.title: Individual Meetings
docs.text:
• One-on-one meetings with Lucie are held regularly, usually on a weekly basis.
  • The exact time and format are arranged individually.

docs.title: On-site Presence
docs.text:
Lab members are expected to be on site on Wednesdays, when lab meetings and joint lab meetings take place.

In addition, lab members are encouraged to be present on days when departmental seminars are scheduled. These events are an important part of the academic environment and provide opportunities for learning and discussion.

docs.title: Data Management
docs.text:
To ensure good research practice and data integrity, lab members should follow these principles:

  • Store raw data separately from processed data
  • Never overwrite raw data
  • Ensure compliance with data protection, data management, and ethics regulations

docs.title: Authorship and Contributions
docs.text:
• Authorship follows standard academic guidelines
  • Authorship and contributions should be discussed early in collaborative projects to ensure transparency and fairness

docs.title: Running Online Experiments
docs.text:
The DM² Lab typically uses Gorilla for running online behavioural experiments.

Gorilla provides a robust platform for experiment building, participant management, and data collection, and supports a wide range of experimental designs commonly used in cognitive and decision-making research.

docs.title: Typical Use Cases
docs.text:
Gorilla is commonly used in the lab for:

  • Online behavioural tasks
  • Controlled experimental workflows
  • Integration with external recruitment platforms (e.g. Prolific)

docs.title: Before Running an Online Experiment
docs.text:
Before launching an online study, ensure that:

  • The task has been thoroughly tested and piloted
  • Instructions are clear, unambiguous, and consistent across conditions
  • All relevant data variables are correctly recorded
  • Consent forms and participant information materials are up to date and approved where required

docs.title: Using Gorilla
docs.text:
Experiments can be created in Gorilla using a combination of built-in tools and custom code.

  • Build or adapt tasks using Gorilla’s task builder and existing task components
  • Where necessary, extend functionality using custom JavaScript code to implement specific experimental logic or dynamic behaviour
  • Use project versioning to track changes during development
  • Test experiments across different browsers and devices
  • Run internal pilot studies before external data collection

docs.title: After Data Collection
docs.text:
After completing data collection:

  • Download and securely store raw data
  • Perform initial quality checks on behavioural data
  • Document task versions, settings, and any changes made during the study

Project-specific Gorilla tasks, scripts, and related materials are maintained via the lab’s GitHub repositories.

docs.title: Projects & GitHub
docs.text:
The DM² Lab maintains all code, analysis pipelines, and project-specific materials on GitHub.

The lab GitHub organisation can be found here: DM² Lab on GitHub

docs.title: Available Repositories
docs.text:
Current repositories include:

  • Wenyu’s Detachment EEG Experiment detachment-eeg-experiment-wenyu-gabor

Additional repositories may be added as projects develop.

docs.title: Good Practice for Lab Projects
docs.text:
Lab members are encouraged to:

  • Use GitHub for version control
  • Document code clearly and consistently
  • Share improvements, fixes, and extensions via pull requests

docs.title: Resources
docs.text:
The DM² Lab makes extensive use of computational modelling approaches to study human decision making and metacognition.

In addition to lab-specific code and experimental protocols, there are a number of high-quality external resources that are useful for building background knowledge and technical skills.

Below we collect learning materials, tutorials, and references that may be helpful for lab members at different stages of their training.

If you come across a resource that you find useful and think it would benefit other lab members, you are very welcome to add it to this page. You should already have permission to edit the lab wiki; if not, please contact Lucie.

docs.title: Neuromatch Academy – Computational Neuroscience
docs.text:
The Neuromatch Academy online course materials provide a comprehensive introduction to computational neuroscience, modelling, and data analysis.

The tutorials are well structured, hands-on, and particularly useful for building intuition about models commonly used in decision-making research.

docs.title: FieldTrip – Advanced Analysis of MEG, EEG, and Invasive Electrophysiological Data
docs.text:
FieldTrip is a widely used open-source MATLAB toolbox for EEG and MEG analysis.

The official FieldTrip tutorials provide step-by-step guidance and best practices for data preprocessing and analysis.

docs.title: MNE-Python Documentation
docs.text:
MNE-Python is an open-source Python package for EEG and MEG analysis.

The documentation includes tutorials, examples, and reproducible workflows covering a wide range of analysis techniques.

docs.title: GitHub Guides – Version Control and Collaboration
docs.text: The official GitHub Guides cover version control, collaboration, and best practices for managing research code and working effectively with GitHub.

docs.title: Softwares
docs.text: The DM² Lab uses a range of software tools for experimental design, computational modelling, and neuroimaging data analysis.

docs.title: MATLAB
docs.text:
MATLAB is widely used in the lab for behavioural experiments, computational modelling, and EEG data analysis.

Queen Mary University of London provides free access to MATLAB for staff and students via the MathWorks Total Academic Headcount (TAH) program: MathWorks TAH – QMUL

When working on shared projects, please ensure that you are using the correct MATLAB version and required toolboxes.

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
Python is commonly used in the lab for computational modelling, data analysis, and data visualisation.

Project-specific dependencies should be documented clearly and managed using appropriate environment tools (e.g. virtual environments or environment configuration files).

docs.title: R
docs.text:
R is used in the lab for statistical analysis, modelling, and data visualisation, particularly in exploratory analyses.

Most R-based analyses are typically written and run using RStudio, which provides a convenient integrated development environment for scripting, data visualisation, and reproducible analysis.

When collaborating, ensure that analysis scripts are well documented and that package versions are specified where relevant.

docs.title: Neuroimaging Analysis Toolkits
docs.text:
The lab uses established open-source toolkits for EEG and neuroimaging analysis. The choice of toolkit depends on the project and analysis requirements.

  • FieldTrip MATLAB-based toolbox for EEG and MEG analysis.

  • MNE-Python Python-based toolbox for EEG and MEG analysis.
